newsitem.title: USA: CBOT July/November soy spread jumps on export talk.
newsitem.headline: CBOT July/November soy spread jumps on export talk.

text.p: The July/November soybean spread at the Chicago Board of Trade reversed a three-week trend and widened sharply on Friday on ideas demand for old crop supplies was again growing too fast, analysts said.

"The bull spreads will continue to work as long as soybean crush and export sales continue to run over 30 million bushels," said Joel Karlin, analyst with Everen Securities in Chicago. "It's that simple. The talk of China was friendly and last night's crush wasn't too bad."
Exporters said China apparently made a snap purchase of one to three U.S. soybean cargoes for May shipment overnight.
"We were aware of one FOB trade," said one exporter. "We were told delivery was set for May/July. Perhaps the Chinese are long beans."
The China talk, at a time Brazilian beans are still cheaper than U.S., was enough to rally old crop sharply.

At 1155 CDT, the July/November soybean spread was trading at $1.72 per bushel, premium July. That was 19 cents higher than Thursday's closing spread. The spread had narrowed for three weeks since peaking at $1.86-3/4 per bushel on April 2.
Analysts were hesitant to predict where the spread would go from here.
New-crop U.S. soybeans have not yet been planted, so weather concerns could send November futures higher.
But the talk of Chinese demand rekindled ideas that prices had not risen enough to ration tight U.S. soybean supplies.
The U.S. Agriculture Department earlier this month projected marketing year ending soybean stocks at September 1 would total 125 million bushels versus 183 million last year.

The National Oilseed Processors Association on Thursday put weekly soybean crushings at 25.64 million bushels, in line with trade ideas. But analysts said the crush needs to fall below 25 million bushels to ensure adequate year-end supplies.
"That's in the trade's mind now," said Dave Armstrong, analyst with ABN-AMRO Chicago Corp, referring to ideas nearby demand remained too strong for remaining soybean supplies.

"The signs (of strong demand) are the big March crush (U.S. Census) that was reported yesterday, less slowdown than people were calling for in the weekly crush, strong basis in the eastern Corn Belt and continued strong export sales," Armstrong added.
The U.S. Census Bureau on Thursday said soybean crushing in March rose to 130 million bushels, up from 125 million in February and compared to 115 million crushed in March 1996.
Big soybean plantings this year still weigh on Nov beans.
The USDA expects 68.8 million acres planted to soybeans this year, against 64.21 million last year.

"We're looking at real rapid corn planting and that bodes well for rapid soybean planting," Armstrong added. "You're not getting better in the Nov very quickly here, yet the nearby can rock and roll."

Bill Biedermann, director of research at Allendale Inc, said the retracement in July and the spread seen earlier this month was tied in part to news that at least one U.S. firm was importing soybeans from Brazil.
Such imports helped ease concern that tight U.S. supplies would not last through the summer.

"The reason it sold off over the last three weeks was over this import business," Biedermann said. "I think that really smooths the timetable of shortages out. It could push that essential critical time frame out to August."
